verses.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Behold, I have made you as God to Pharaoh; and Aaron your brother shall be your prophet.
You shall speak all that I command you; and Aaron your brother shall speak to Pharaoh, that he let the children of Israel go out of his land.
I will harden Pharaoh’s heart, and multiply my signs and my wonders in the land of Egypt.
But Pharaoh will not listen to you, and I will lay my hand on Egypt, and bring out my armies, my people the children of Israel, out of the land of Egypt by great judgments.
The Egyptians shall know that I am Yahweh, when I stretch out my hand on Egypt, and bring out the children of Israel from among them.”
Moses and Aaron did so. As Yahweh commanded them, so they did.
Moses was eighty years old, and Aaron eighty-three years old, when they spoke to Pharaoh.
Yahweh spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying,
“When Pharaoh speaks to you, saying, ‘Perform a miracle!’ then you shall tell Aaron, ‘Take your rod, and cast it down before Pharaoh, that it become a serpent.’”
Moses and Aaron went in to Pharaoh, and they did so, as Yahweh had commanded: and Aaron cast down his rod before Pharaoh and before his servants, and it became a serpent.
Then Pharaoh also called for the wise men and the sorcerers. They also, the magicians of Egypt, did the same thing with their enchantments.
For they each cast down their rods, and they became serpents: but Aaron’s rod swallowed up their rods.
Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he didn’t listen to them; as Yahweh had spoken.
Yahweh said to Moses, “Pharaoh’s heart is stubborn. He refuses to let the people go.
Go to Pharaoh in the morning. Behold, he goes out to the water; and you shall stand by the river’s bank to meet him; and the rod which was turned to a serpent you shall take in your hand.
You shall tell him, ‘Yahweh, the God of the Hebrews, has sent me to you, saying, “Let my people go, that they may serve me in the wilderness:” and behold, until now you haven’t listened.
Yahweh says, “In this you shall know that I am Yahweh. Behold, I will strike with the rod that is in my hand on the waters which are in the river, and they shall be turned to blood.
The fish that are in the river shall die, and the river shall become foul; and the Egyptians shall loathe to drink water from the river.”’”

Yahweh said to Moses, “Tell Aaron, ‘Take your rod, and stretch out your hand over the waters of Egypt, over their rivers, over their streams, and over their pools, and over all their ponds of water, that they may become blood; and there shall be blood throughout all the land of Egypt, both in vessels of wood and in vessels of stone.’”

Moses and Aaron did so, as Yahweh commanded; and he lifted up the rod, and struck the waters that were in the river, in the sight of Pharaoh, and in the sight of his servants; and all the waters that were in the river were turned to blood.
The fish that were in the river died; and the river became foul, and the Egyptians couldn’t drink water from the river; and the blood was throughout all the land of Egypt.
The magicians of Egypt did the same thing with their enchantments; and Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he didn’t listen to them; as Yahweh had spoken.
Pharaoh turned and went into his house, and he didn’t even take this to heart.
All the Egyptians dug around the river for water to drink; for they couldn’t drink the river water.
Seven days were fulfilled, after Yahweh had struck the river.

footnotes.content: What a promise: God makes Moses as a god to Pharaoh. Not by power of arms but by the authority God grants. I've learned that real authority flows from obedience to the Lord, not from the strength we carry in ourselves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses is to speak what God commands; Aaron becomes his voice to the throne. Even the stammering are eloquent when they speak God's word. How often have I seen the Lord use faithful lips, not clever ones, to move mountains?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God will harden Pharaoh's heart and multiply His signs. I've watched the Lord do this in my own time—He doesn't leave us guessing. His works grow clearer as He speaks, even if the proud refuse to listen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God's hand will lay hold of Egypt through great judgments—a word that echoes through Scripture as God's way of redeeming His people. The plagues are not mere punishment but a rescue story written in signs.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When the Egyptians know that He is Yahweh, the whole earth will know His name. The deliverance of one people becomes testimony to all. I pray I'm always watching to see how the Lord displays His glory in my neighbors' sight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses and Aaron did so. No hesitation, no negotiation—just obedience. That simplicity haunts me in the best way. How many times have I delayed the Lord's work by asking too many questions first?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses was eighty, Aaron eighty-three—already old by any measure, yet the Lord calls them to a brand-new work. He is not bound by our calendars or what we think our seasons should hold.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying—the word comes before the work. I've noticed that God always gives instruction before asking for faith. That steadies me when the next hard thing arrives.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When Pharaoh asks for a miracle, Aaron is told what to do. The rod becoming a serpent is not magic but obedience—God working through a tool held by a faithful hand. I wonder how many times I've missed seeing God's power because I was looking for flash instead of faithfulness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Aaron cast down his rod and it became a serpent in front of all eyes. Sometimes the Lord's greatest works happen in the most public places, where the proud can see and still refuse. That teaches me something about the hardness human hearts can reach.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh called the wise men and sorcerers—the magicians of Egypt. In Scripture, these are the pattern of human wisdom set against God's truth. They appear to match God's power but always fall short.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Each magician cast down his rod and it became a serpent—but Aaron's rod swallowed them all. A small thing, a telling thing. God's work doesn't just match the world's counterfeit; it consumes it. I pray for eyes to see the difference.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh's heart was hardened; he didn't listen. Even after seeing God's power exceed the magicians, his will stayed locked. It reminds me that no sign, however clear, can force a stubborn heart toward God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God tells Moses what He already knows: Pharaoh's heart is stubborn, he refuses to let the people go. Before the blow falls, the Lord speaks plainly about it. His word and His work are never out of step.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Go to Pharaoh in the morning, at the water—a time and place of significance in the ancient world. The Nile was Egypt's lifeline; the river's edge was where power met its source. God chooses the moment and the place where the blow will land.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh, the God of the Hebrews, has sent me—a declaration of identity. God names Himself by His relationship to His people. That name carries both an invitation and a warning for all who hear it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: I will strike the river with this rod, and the waters shall turn to blood. Water is life; making it blood is a sign that touches every Egyptian's deepest need. The Lord strikes not to destroy but to open eyes to who He is.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The fish will die, the river will stink, the people will loathe to drink. Sometimes I miss that God doesn't just make a point—He makes it impossible to ignore. When the Lord speaks through consequence, He speaks a language everyone understands.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Stretch your hand over every water in Egypt—the rivers, streams, pools, and ponds, even the water in wooden and stone vessels. God's judgment is thorough, reaching into every corner of daily life. Nothing is outside His reach or His purpose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses and Aaron did so, as Yahweh commanded—they lifted the rod and struck in the sight of all. When God's servants obey, the Lord takes full responsibility for the outcome. The power was never in their hands; it was always in His name.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The river became foul; the Egyptians couldn't drink. At this moment, the whole land knew the God of the Hebrews had moved. Yet Pharaoh's heart was already turning away from what his own eyes could see. Pride is a deeper blindness than any plague.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even the magicians did the same with their enchantments—turned water to blood—and still Pharaoh didn't listen. When a man is determined to see lies, he will find a sorcerer ready to tell them. Lord, keep my heart from such deafness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh turned and went into his house, didn't even take it to heart. What hardness of spirit it takes to walk away from such a sign. He had water turning to blood, and he chose to go home and pretend it didn't matter.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All the Egyptians dug around the river for water to drink. Even in judgment, God leaves room for survival; the people could find water if they looked. There's mercy in the very consequence—space to live, if we'll accept what the Lord is saying.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seven days were fulfilled after the river was struck—readers today hear an echo in that number. When God speaks through time itself, even days become a kind of word. Looking back from now, I'm grateful the Lord's patience with us is measured in seasons too, not just the hardness of any single moment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
